title: Strategy beyond the battlefield
note: The same habits that serve generals serve leaders anywhere: match ends, ways and means; decide under uncertainty without fooling yourself; negotiate from interests and a strong walk-away option; and compete by choosing where you can win, using tools such as Porter's five forces, generic strategies and SWOT.

read.title: From the battlefield to the boardroom
text: Strategy begins with three questions: what are we trying to achieve, how will we achieve it, and with what resources? Planners call these ends, ways and means. Many failures, in war and in business, come from a mismatch, such as grand goals pursued with too few resources, or busy activity that serves no clear end.

Decisions are made under uncertainty, so good strategists think in probabilities. They weigh outcomes by their likelihood, update estimates when new evidence arrives, and guard against familiar traps: anchoring on the first number heard, favoring evidence that confirms what they already believe, and throwing more money after a failing project because so much has already been spent.

In negotiation, the key source of strength is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement, or BATNA. If you can walk away to something good, you can bargain firmly. Skilled negotiators also look past stated positions to the interests underneath, which often reveals deals that leave both sides better off.

In markets, Michael Porter urged firms to study the forces shaping their industry, rivals, new entrants, substitutes, suppliers and buyers, and then choose a clear path: lowest cost, a distinctive product, or a focused niche. Like Sun Tzu's ideal general, the best competitor often wins by choosing a field where a head-on fight is unnecessary.

q.q: What causes many strategic failures, according to the reading?
o: A mismatch between ends, ways and means

q.q: What lets a negotiator bargain firmly?
o: A good alternative if talks fail

q.q: Which choice did Porter urge firms to make?
o: Compete on every front at once
Lowest cost, a distinctive product, or a focused niche
